item.title: PM Carney says Canada intends to match U.S. tariffs ‘dollar for dollar,’ after suspending trade negotiations
item.description: A new round of punishing U.S. tariffs on Canada went into effect early Saturday morning, as the two countries failed to reach a deal ahead of the midnight deadline.
item.dc:creator: CTVNews.ca Staff
item.content:encoded: A new round of punishing U.S. tariffs on Canada went into effect early Saturday morning, as Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended trade negotiations minutes before the deadline. The announcement came following a three-day extension given by U.S. President Donald Trump to give trade representatives from both sides more time to negotiate a deal. The 50 per cent tariffs target US$20 billion worth of Canadian goods, including cement and hockey sticks. Here is everything that happened on Aug. 21: PM Carney says Canada intends to match the U.S. tariffs ‘dollar for dollar’ Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office released a statement ahead of the deadline saying he suspended trade negotiations with the United States, setting in motion the 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods. “I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed Canada’s negotiators to return to Ottawa. They have worked hard, in good faith, to defend the interests of Canadians throughout these negotiations up until the very last minute,” the PMO said in the statement. “However, last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.” “At midnight tonight, the U.S. intends to impose a 50% tariff on roughly $28 billion of Canadian goods,” the statement read. “Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses.” Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca Journalist Canada has declined to finalize the trade deal, ‘upended’ balance: Greer In a statement released Friday night, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Canada has declined to finalize the deal and “upended” the balance reached during the negotiations. “Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walkbacks of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days,” the statement said. “In addition, Canada is continuing to maintain its prolonged retaliation against the United States, including, among other things, flat-out prohibitions on certain American goods and services.” The statement went on to say that Canada declined the deal despite the U.S. offering Canada “better treatment” and “significant tariff reductions” on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber in exchange for concessions. “The U.S. offer was also forward-looking and included a historic economic and national security partnership to cooperate on export controls, combat transshipment, enhance digital trade, and align certain external tariffs,” Greer said in the statement. “This is a missed opportunity for Canada to partner with the United States, which is the fastest-growing economy in the G7.” Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca Journalist ‘Tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar’:  Ford extends support for prime minister Ontario Premier Doug Ford extended his support for Prime Minister Mark Carney in a social media post, after the trade negotiations were suspended Friday night. “Team Canada needs to stand together more united than ever before,” Ford said. “The prime minister has my full support for a strong response—tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar. As we fight to protect Canadian sovereignty and economic security, everything needs to be on the table. Ontario is ready to do its part.” Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca Journalist ‘We’ll keep fighting’: Eby B.C. Premier David Eby, who was advocating for relief on softwood lumber tariffs, also responded to the news, saying Canada’s “politeness should never be mistaken for weakness.” “We didn’t ask for this, but we’ll keep fighting for as long as it takes,” Eby added. Stephanie Ha, CTV News’ Ottawa News Bureau manager As tariff deadline approaches, dynamic ‘not going well:’ sources With less than two hours until new 50 per cent tariffs are set to be imposed on a variety of Canadian goods, two sources close to the negotiations tell CTV News that there are some challenges with the dynamic in negotiations, particularly with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick who is involved in the final hours of talks. According to the sources, the talks are focused on “just a couple” of outstanding issues, but some of the personal dynamics with Lutnick, who appears to have lingering feelings over recent issues with the Gordie Howe International Bridge, is a challenge. The opening of the bridge was delayed for weeks because of U.S. complaints over toll governance and revenue sharing, after which Canada agreed to share revenues earlier than planned. Canada’s chief trade negotiator Janice Charette remains at the United States Representative’s office in Washington as of late Friday night as talks continue. Stephanie Ha, CTV News’ Ottawa News Bureau manager With files from CTV’s Chief Political Correspondent Vassy Kapelos and CTV’s Senior Political Correspondent Mike Le Couteur ‘Working up until the last minute’: LeBlanc “We have more work to do,” LeBlanc told reporters as he exited the U.S. trade representatives office around 7:30 p.m. on Friday. “We’re going to continue working up until the last minute. Our job is not finished. Canadian workers, Canadian businesses expect us to do all of this important work” he said. Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist ‘I only make good deals,’ Trump says “I only make good deals,” Trump told reporters on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland. He was asked about progress toward a deal with Canada. He said talks were “moving along,” and that his team has a “good relationship” with Carney. He didn’t offer details on the prospective deal. “We have to take care of our farmers.” Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist A ‘low-key horrible’ deal: trade policy expert Some concern about the deal still persists, an international trade policy researcher told CTV News Channel. “For some of the leaks we’ve seen, it doesn’t sound like it’s going to be a good deal,” Stuart Trew said hours before the deadline on Friday. “In fact, as my niece might say, it sounds ‘pretty low-key horrible’” Trew said, referring to tariffs that will remain on steel exports to the U.S. “Aluminum (and) the auto tariffs, at least according to the leaks, being at 15 per cent would be – in the short-to-medium term – pretty unsustainable for the industry.” Trew said such a deal would inevitably “eat into the reason to make any vehicles in Canada whatsoever.” He cautioned against putting Canada in a worse position than before the trade war started by accepting a deal that would put U.S. booze back on the shelves and letting go of our retaliatory tariffs. “The legitimate question is why would we come to such a bad deal now, when all we’re getting out of this is some kind of barely noticeable reprieve, right?” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist ‘Aiming to get the best agreement’: Alberta’s Smith Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is optimistic for a new trade deal with the United States, telling CTV News Calgary the best deal for Canada would involve no additional tariffs. “I know everybody hopes that we could get 100 per cent of all products going across the border tariff free,” Smith said in an interview. “But I think where we’re at in the negotiations is that we’re aiming to get the best agreement in the world of any nation with the United States and a reduction in the current tariffs that we have.” It’s the first time Smith has spoken on the intense negotiations between Ottawa and Washington during trade deadline week. Cassidy McMackon, CTV News Calgary, Digital Producer Compromise a ‘hallmark’ of any good deal: former U.S. ambassador to Canada For any good deal, there need to be concessions on both sides, according to former U.S. ambassador to Canada David L. Cohen. Cohen told CTV News Channel Friday night that he has been “optimistic,” throughout the process and that although it might take both, Canada and the U.S. some time to reach an agreement, there will ultimately be one. However, he said the “hallmark” of a good deal is when there is “some unhappiness” on both sides. “There’s a compromise here, and it’s a compromise where Canada is giving something up, but the U.S. is giving something up too,” Cohen said. “Both sides giving something up, both sides being a little unhappy with the landing place, but both sides looking at the bigger picture and understanding that there are huge benefits to both Canada and the U.S. to a resolution of this dispute, which has not benefited either country.” Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca Journalist Trade deal is an ‘economic security negotiation’: analyst Following Trump’s comment that trade talks are moving along, an international trade analyst says securing a deal is now effectively an “economic security negotiation.” “I feel for the number of companies, the factories, and all those that are engaged in looking at this carefully to ensure that they can continue to do business,” Jacques Shore told CTV News Channel on Friday. Canada needs to reach a trade agreement “right now,” to ensure goods currently protected under CUSMA with no tariffs on them “remain as they are without this potential of 50 per cent,” Shore added. Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Trump’s tariffs on autos ‘outrageous’: spokesperson National spokesperson of the Canadian Automobile Dealers Association, Huw Williams believes that Canada and the U.S. should have completely automotive free trade as in the past 60 years but that must be viewed with a “dose of realism” that the other side is an unpredictable and “bombastic” administration. “If the automotive industry remains competitive within the North American context, consumers will be the winner on both sides of the border,” he told CTV News Channel. Williams described U.S. President Trump’s 25 per cent tariffs on autos as “outrageous” which he said is bad for consumers and dealers, both in the U.S and Canada. Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca Journalist Canadian importers need U.S. alcohol: executive Stacy Kyle, executive director of the Import Vintners and Spirits Association, says she’s hoping premiers get American liquor back on store shelves, since is something she’s been asking for since the ban was put in place in March 2025. “The importers are Canadian. They’re locals...and they’ve been impacted by this ban and unable to do business,” Kyle told CTV News Channel on Friday. “So, it’s important for our members to have viable businesses and operations to maintain their relationships they’ve built with their suppliers.” Elianna Lev, CTVNews.ca Journalist We want to hear from you Are you worried about how tariffs might affect your work? Have trade disruptions already impacted your job? Share your story by emailing us at dotcom@bellmedia.ca with your name, general location and phone number in case we want to follow up. Your comments may be used in a CTV News story. Lumber industry needs certainty: expert Executive director of the Independent Wood Processors Association of B.C. says that while he’s pleased softwood lumber has remained on the negotiating table, the industry needs certainty. “Let’s keep in mind we’ve been at this for nine years. We had a tariff that started around eight per cent, now it’s up to 45 per cent and it could expand to 50 per cent,” Brian Menzies told CTV News Channel on Friday. “I don’t think the outcome is going to be great, but at least there’ll be some certainty, and that’s what I want right now for our small businesses,” he said. Menzies said about $11 billion in tariff deposits is currently being held at the border, and many small businesses have taken on significant financial risk, including using their homes as collateral to cover the required bonds. “They want to see some resolution to this. They want to see some of those deposits returned to them as well because they have been paying it out of their own pocket to survive right now.” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Canadian team takes ‘working lunch’: source A source from the Canadian team tells CTV News LeBlanc, Charette, Blanchard and Wiseman are participating in a “working lunch.” Mike Le Couteur, Senior Political Correspondent LeBlanc returns LeBlanc just passed news cameras on his way back into the U.S. Trade Representative’s office for the first time since departing for lunch at around 1:20 p.m. ET – more than two hours ago. He did not stop to speak to media. Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist ‘It’s tricky for Mark Carney’: Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney, the former premier of Alberta, says while trade talks appear to be going “in a pretty good direction,” he has concerns. “I just hope that our government hasn’t made all sorts of preliminary concessions, and I say preliminary because this is an appetizer for the main meal, which is the CUSMA negotiation or renewal,” he told CTV News Channel on Friday. Although Carney is well-equipped to handle negotiations, he is ultimately in a tough position explains Kenney. “It’s tricky for Mark Carney. It couldn’t be trickier,” he said. Kenney said the prime minister is likely torn between his commitment to aggressively defend the interests of Canadians’ in sectors including auto, while also creating “a space of some stability, knowing full well that based on past actions, the Trump administration could just do a 180 all over again.” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist LeBlanc has entered the building LeBlanc has entered the U.S. Trade Representatives office. He did not stop to take questions from reporters. Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist Negotiations may be ‘phased’ With hours left to deadline, a trade lawyer says Canadian and U.S. representatives may extended negotiations through the weekend and opt for a “phased approach.” “There is going to be a good amount of negotiation left,” Robert Glasgow, international trade lawyer, told CTV News Channel on Friday. “I think they’re almost certainly going to start segmenting it down ... but that’s probably going to take a few more days to negotiate,” he added. The deal won’t eliminate tariffs entirely, Glasgow said, and Carney’s team is likely focused on preserving the CUSMA exemption and “drive tariffs as low as he can on as broad of a basis as he can get it.” Under the CUSMA exemption, goods that comply with CUSMA rules of origin are generally exempt from U.S. blanket or general emergency tariffs. While Carney has partially pivoted defence procurement to some European contractors, he will want to service “that segment with multinational and transnational participation of Canadian firms.” “If we can focus on procuring from American companies that are producing domestically, we still retain that ... procurement base, while still potentially placating the demands of the American administration,” Glasgow said. Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist Trade talks today This morning’s meeting between Canadian and American negotiators is expected to take place at 11:30 a.m., according to a source close to the talks. Canada-U.S. Trade Minister LeBlanc, Chief Trade Negotiator Janice Charette and Carney’s Chief of Staff Marc-Andre Blanchard, are expected to attend. Mike Le Couteur, Senior Political Correspondent and Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist Deadline could be extended: political analyst A former Trudeau staff member says that while a deal is hopefully signed tonight, she would not be surprised if the tariff deadline was extended again. “We’re seeing a level of diffusion come out,” Sharan Kaur, former deputy chief of staff to former finance minister Bill Morneau, told CTV News Channel on Friday. The U.S. president, the now-CTV News political analyst added, is known for making “flippant comments” when things aren’t going his way. She also pointed to issues discussed this week like returning U.S. alcohol to Canadian stores. “These concessions ... are leverage,” she said. “... We have to get used to the fact that tariffs are going to be around in one way, shape or form. This is actually a positive discussion taking place.” Canadians aren’t the only ones impacted; Trump also needs the deal, Kaur said. “The whole anti-everything American sentiment ... is impacting them,” she said. “...Let’s also keep in mind that he’s got midterms coming up.” It’s difficult to say if the deal could be trusted, she said. “He is known to rip deals, left, right and centre.” “The goal is to ensure that the temperature is brought down and that they get to a point where industry is not suffering.” Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist This won’t be an ‘early night’ An international trade lawyer says he’s anticipating being up all night as he awaits final details from the Canadian government. “Let’s put this way: I don’t think I’m going to have an early night,” Barry Appleton told CTV News on Friday. “But here’s the good part: they’re walking in the room. They’re still going to have more talks.” Appleton said that the problem with the trade deal after Trump’s three-day reprieve is that it will likely leave numerous items unresolved. “This is just a deal to get us talking again to have more of a deal, and what are we going to give up to have that? Right, that’s the question that we all want to know. And there’s so many different ideas circulating. That’s the part we got to figure out,” he said. Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Poilievre to Carney: ‘Don’t take a bad deal’ Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre repeated his call Friday for Prime Minister Mark Carney not to “take a bad deal.” “Mr. Carney promised in the last election that he would be elbows up. He promised that he would negotiate a win,” Poilievre said in a press conference in Kitchener, Ont. on Friday. “In his words, he promised, and I quote, that he could ‘handle Trump.’ He promised he would not accept a bad deal. Mr. Carney, keep your promise. Fight for Canada.” Asked by reporters if it’s acceptable for Canada to agree to a reduced tariffs on steel and aluminum, Poilievre said “no, absolutely not.” “One-sided tariffs on Canadian industry would be a bad deal,” he added. Stephanie Ha, CTV News’ Ottawa News Bureau manager Booze ban ‘had its time’: Raitt The decision to reverse provincial bans on U.S. alcohol may be the reason Canada secures a deal tonight, says Lisa Raitt, member of the Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations and former deputy leader of the Conservative Party of Canada. She said Trump has made it very clear that he views the removal of American alcohol from Canadian store shelves as a discriminatory measure, and as a result, threatened 50 per cent tariffs on vulnerable industries. “You have to do whatever you can to ensure that that didn’t happen, and that doesn’t happen tonight,” said Raitt. “Asking the premiers to reverse their booze bans, I do believe, is an important part of the entire deal.” She says while the alcohol ban was effective in getting U.S. attention, “it had its time.” “The reality is that the leverage on this negotiation going around really did come from the U.S.,” says Raitt. She says tariff pressure forced the two countries into important negotiations that have likely yielded results and “hopefully a deal that both sides can live with and can prosper with going forward.” Anam Khan, BNN Bloomberg journalist The ‘best deal’ for autos Canada is in a position to get “the best deal” for its auto industry compared to the rest of the world, according to an industry representative. Huw Williams, spokesperson for the Canadian Automobile Dealers Association, told CTV News Channel on Thursday that there is opportunity to get “a good short term deal that hopefully rolls into the CUSMA negotiations in the future.” Canada is the biggest customer of U.S.-made vehicles, he said. “It doesn’t do well to attack your customer.” Williams said they have asked their U.S. counterparts to communicate that the tariffs hurt the economy on both sides. Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist TSX shows gains The S&P/TSX composite was up nearly a point (36,694, up 0.88 per cent) in Friday morning trading. Energy and mining stocks showed the largest gains. Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist Anand talks Arctic, NATO with Rubio While Canadian and U.S. negotiators hammer out the details of a deal, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand met with her American counterpart, Marco Rubio, for security talks today. A readout from Anand’s office reports the two discussed “transnational fraudulent activity including scam centres,” Arctic foreign policy and NATO investments. “Minister Anand highlighted that Canada will continue to engage constructively with the United States on trade and to strengthen our economic relationship,” the statement added. Canada recently committed to spend five per cent of its GDP on defence by 2035. U.S. President Donald Trump has long pushed allied countries to increase their military investments. Anand and Rubio will speak again in September at the United Nations. Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist PM tried to ‘out-tough’ Trump: Vance U.S. Vice-President JD Vance said Carney tried to “out-tough” Trump in trade negotiations and credited Conservative MP Jamil Jivani as an “effective advocate” in the deal talks. In audio from a Wednesday fundraiser in Southampton, N.Y., which was provided to The Canadian Press by a source who attended the private function, Vance said Carney is a “very sweet guy” and he gets along with him quite well. But Carney “comes in and puffs his chest out and says, ‘I’m going to, like, out-tough Donald Trump,’” he added. “It’s hilarious because Carney presents this as some victory for Canada when fundamentally, like, they climb down on a lot of issues,” Vance told the room. “But the quiet sort of behind-the-scenes story is that this, like, random MP who has a good relationship with us has been a pretty effective advocate,” he said about Jivani. Vance added there’s “this guy Pierre Poilievre, who is the leader of the Conservatives in Canada,” adding he is a “non-entity” in negotiations. The White House and the vice-president’s office have not yet responded to a request for comment. The Canadian Press. Read the full story here. Vance’s comments are ‘childish,’ says ex-ambassador Vance’s comments about Carney were “childish” and “flippant,” according to Gordon D. Giffen, who served as U.S. Ambassador to Canada from 1997 to 2001. “The vice-president was out of line,” he told CTV News Channel from Brevard, N.C. Asked what Canada should do next if a deal isn’t reached, Giffen said he doesn’t think the U.S. will follow through with imposing the 50 per cent tariffs as the president promised. He called the new, 50 per cent tariffs “unsound, bad policy,” and predicted their imposition would beget further Canadian retaliation. Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist Winery owner unconcerned about U.S. booze return An Ontario winery owner says he isn’t worried about a drop in sales should U.S. booze return to store shelves. Donald Ziraldo, who is the founding chairman of the Vintners Quality Alliance (VQA), told CTV Your Morning on Friday that provincial bans have boosted sales at local wineries by 25 per cent to 100 per cent. “People became more aware ... that the Niagara Canadian wines, in particular, are as good as the California, and probably a little bit less expensive,” he said. Prime Minister Mark Carney asked premiers this week to lift their respective bans, which have been in place since February 2025. All have said they will comply. The VQA is Canada’s Canada’s official regulatory and appellation of origin system for high-quality wines. A VQA label guarantees that a wine is made entirely from locally grown grapes in Ontario or B.C. and meets strict production and labeling standards. Ziraldo added that he hopes Quebec and the Maritime provinces will join the alliance to let consumers know which wines are “100 per cent grown in Canada.” Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist Sustainable profit margin a good deal for auto makers Flavio Volpe, the president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers Association, said a good deal for his members is one that allows auto makers to have a sustainable profit margin. “I think a lot of people who aren’t as familiar with the industry say, ‘Hey, look, if you go down from 25 to 15 (per cent tariffs), that sounds great,’” he told CTV News Channel on Friday. However Volpe elaborated that even if U.S. tariffs on Canadian autos fall from 25 per cent to 15 per cent, that may not be enough to protect Canadian carmakers especially after being targeted “by Donald Trump’s White House and also our other main competitors, China, at the same time.” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist LeBlanc on trade deal: ‘We’re very close’ Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc shared an update following a more than three-hour meeting with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in Washington on Thursday, saying they are “very close” to an agreement. “We continue to make progress, and we’re going to stay here and do the work that’s necessary until we get to that point,” LeBlanc said to reporters, while also describing the meeting as “long” and “detailed.” Chief Trade Negotiator Janice Charette, Canadian Ambassador to the U.S. Mark Wiseman and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Chief of Staff Marc-André Blanchard were also involved in the meeting. Stephanie Ha, bureau manager, Ottawa News Bureau All provinces agreed to restock U.S. liquor: N.L. premier Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham says Canada’s premiers have agreed to return U.S. alcohol to store shelves as part of the tentative trade deal with the U.S. He said the prime minister is confident an agreement will be reached and that “as part of this agreement, he asked all of the provinces, as a sign of good faith, ‘would we put U.S. liquor back on our shelves,’ and we all agreed.” Several of the premiers have not commented publicly on the issue. U.S. alcohol products remain off the shelves in every province except Alberta and Saskatchewan. Tiffany Hendsbee, CTV News supervising multiplatform writer

item.title: Transat’s fuel costs surge by over $100 million as Iran war takes ongoing toll
item.description: The parent company of Air Transat says it paid $105 million in additional jet fuel costs in the third quarter compared with a year ago due to higher prices.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: MONTREAL — The parent company of Air Transat paid more than ever for jet fuel in its latest quarter due to the ripple effects of the Iran war, prompting the company to seek further federal aid. The cost of fuel bought by Transat A.T. Inc. climbed by $105 million in the three months ended July 31, compared with a year earlier, the travel company said. The amount also marked a 50 per cent increase from the additional expense Transat paid in the preceding second quarter, according to chief executive Annick Guérard. Combined, the two quarters saw the Montreal-based company pay an extra $175 million for the refined kerosene that powers its 42 planes. For an outfit that made $242 million in total last year — and that lost nearly $140 million in 2023 and 2024 combined — the expense stands out on the income statement. Blue skies have yet to emerge for airlines. Energy market volatility is expected to keep up the pressure on jet fuel costs across the industry, the company said. In North America, jet fuel costs nearly US$160 per barrel, up almost 75 per cent from the year before, according to the International Air Transport Association. However, prices are down from their April peaks. Transat’s ability to pass higher fuel costs on to passengers remains “very limited,” the company said in a statement. As a result, it is in talks with the federal government “to explore potential solutions.” Last month, Transat secured up to $150 million in federal aid to help offset the soaring price of jet fuel. At first, customers could stomach the increased fares that resulted, which roughly balanced out the spike in fuel expenses, Guérard told analysts on a second-quarter conference call earlier this summer. “But more recent increases resulted in a slowdown in the booking momentum ... the demand went down,” prompting the airline to tamp down fares and remove some fees, she said on June 11. The size of Transat’s loan from July will be based on the difference in the cost of fuel in the window between late July and Oct. 31 and the same period last year. The financial relief came less than two months after Ottawa announced a loan lifeline available to airlines struggling to cope with sky-high oil prices and the slashed flight schedules and lower profit forecasts that followed. Air Canada suggested earlier in the summer it would not need to draw on the aid, while WestJet said it “strongly opposes” the move because of its market-distorting effects. Headwinds closer to home have also taken a toll. All three airlines have indefinitely suspended all flights and vacation packages to Cuba as the country grapples with an increasingly desperate fuel shortage triggered by a U.S. oil blockade. Cuba marks a major market for Transat, which is a popular destination for Canadians. About 861,000 Canadians visited the island in 2024, according to the country’s statistics office. Trips there accounted for nine per cent of Transat’s flights in the first half of 2025, with Cuba particularly popular among vacationers in Quebec, Transat’s home base. The airline first halted Cuba voyages in mid-February. Air Transat, like most other Canadian carriers, also slashed its flight capacity to the U.S. after demand plummeted following the election of President Donald Trump. Last month, Air Transat cancelled a weekly Halifax-Fort Lauderdale, Fla., route and five-days-a-week service between Montreal and Fort Lauderdale for the upcoming winter season. That left the thrice weekly Quebec City-Fort Lauderdale route as Air Transat’s only service between Canada and a U.S. state. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 21, 2026.

item.title: Possible new Roots owner threads plan for global growth
item.description: Roots Corp.’s likely new U.S. owner wants to take the storied Canadian brand and export it to the rest of the world.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — The New York brand management firm that has signed an agreement to buy Roots Corp. wants to take the storied Canadian brand and export it to the rest of the world. If the proposed deal goes through, Marquee Brands, the firm behind Martha Stewart, Laura Ashley and Roberto Cavalli, says growth will be a top priority. Chief executive Heath Golden said Friday that he envisions his company bringing Roots to big markets like Korea, India and Mexico and expanding the small presence it already has in the U.S. and China. “Many of our partners around the world want to be a part of bringing Roots into different markets,” he said in an interview. “So we think the sky is the limit for this brand.” Roots has more than 100 corporate-owned stores in Canada but just two in the U.S., where it’s been working to expand. A partner operates another 100 shops in Asia and the brand also has a presence on Tmall, Alibaba Group’s popular Chinese platform.  But Golden won’t just lean on global markets for growth. He also wants Roots to build out its home, camping and hospitality businesses without forgetting, well, its roots. The retailer was started by Michigan natives Michael Budman and Don Green, who met at an Ontario summer camp in the sixties and decided to open what eventually became Roots north of the border in 1973. The brand, which sells apparel like sweatpants and leather accessories including bags, has since become a beloved symbol of Canadiana. “The DNA of the brand is incredible,” said Golden, who labelled himself a “longtime admirer of Roots and father of two girls who have the company’s clothing in their closets. “It is loved in its home market and it is loved around the world, so nothing here is broken. This is really about just continuing to build it out.” He offered his insights into Marquee’s hopes for the brand a day after Roots announced it has agreed to be acquired for $4.10 per share in cash — the result of a strategic review the retailer kicked off in March. Its shares were up more than 10 per cent or roughly 35 cents to $4.06 in afternoon trading Friday. The deal still needs shareholder and regulatory approval but if it proceeds, Marquee will use JM&A Design and Development Inc. to develop, manufacture and distribute Roots clothing for Canadian and U.S. stores.  JM&A is led by Joseph Mimran, the Canadian fashion visionary behind Joe Fresh, Club Monaco and Alfred Sung. He’s also the chairman of hat brand Tilley Endurables, clothing retailer Kit and Ace and toy shop Mastermind Toys. Mimran was drawn to the partnership, in part because of how involved Marquee gets in its brands. “When you have a partner like that, as opposed to somebody who just looks at a brand as a cash cow, it makes a huge difference,” he said in the same interview with Golden.  “This is a very emotional brand. It’s an emotional brand for Canada and if you don’t have vested emotional owners, this thing can go terribly wrong.” For now, it appears the two are on the same page, sharing a goal of figuring out how they can best steward the brand but also tailor it to a global audience. It’s a lofty task, Mimran admits, but one he feels more than prepared for, especially because founder Green sent him a “beautiful” note expressing confidence in the arrangement. “I always feel pressure,” Mimran said. “This is a pressure-filled industry. It’s season by season, it’s a product at a time, but I’ve been doing it for a long time.” The key will be nailing the product side of the business because that’s what customers care about, Mimran said. While the specifics of how the brand could transform under its possible new ownership are still taking shape, Roots CEO Meghan Roach signalled she doesn’t expect anything dramatic. “I don’t think you’re going to see a Roots brand that doesn’t look like the brand you expect,” she said.  “I think you’re going to see this team putting in place a lot of exciting things that are going to bring the brand forward in really good ways.” Roach and Golden demurred when asked if she’d be staying in the top role following a sale. Roach said it was too early for such decisions. She joined Roots as interim chief financial officer about seven years ago, rising later to its top job.  Before that, Roach had worked at private equity firm Searchlight Capital Partners L.P., which bought a majority stake in Roots from its founders in 2015. Under Roach, the goal was to return the retailer to a position of strength. She worked to do that by moving the retailer away from markdowns and fashioning itself into more of a prestige brand that occasionally partnered with popular franchises like the Toronto Blue Jays and Toronto Tempo. The new owners will likely find they have to sharpen the company’s product assortment even further to grow its store count and expand its wholesale business, said Liza Amlani, co-founder of the Retail Strategy Group. “This is less about reinventing Roots and more about giving customers what they want from a Canadian brand — elevated fabrics, stores that are exciting and a relevant assortment that they would actually want,” she said in an email. She thinks the biggest risk they run is diluting the brand, which often happens to heritage companies when they expand too broadly or focus too heavily on short-term growth. But if they can keep focused, Amlani thinks the partnership will work. “JM&A has a proven track record of building commercially successful brands,” she said. “Marquee has the money to make it happen.” --- Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 21, 2026.
